    Comparing forecasting models¶

    Which model should you use to forecast your time series: machine learning, a statistical model, a foundation model or a neural network? This guide answers the question with data. The main model families available in skforecast are evaluated with the same backtesting on three datasets with different characteristics:

    Family Model Forecaster
    Baseline Seasonal naive ForecasterEquivalentDate
    Machine learning (linear) Ridge ForecasterRecursive, ForecasterRecursiveMultiSeries
    Machine learning (trees) LightGBM ForecasterRecursive, ForecasterRecursiveMultiSeries
    Foundation Chronos-2 small (zero-shot) ForecasterFoundation
    Statistical AutoARIMA, AutoETS ForecasterStats
    Deep learning LSTM ForecasterRnn

    For each model, the guide reports the accuracy of the point forecast, the calibration of its 80% prediction interval and the computation time.

    Key takeaways¶

    Family Where it stood out in this guide What to keep in mind
    Machine learning (LightGBM, Ridge) The most accurate model with exogenous variables and several years of history. As a global model, it learns the patterns shared by many series in seconds. Its accuracy depends on the features (lags, calendar, exogenous variables) and the hyperparameters. Its intervals need out-of-sample residuals to be well calibrated.
    Foundation (Chronos-2) The most accurate model with the short series and with many series, and close to the best with exogenous variables, without any training. Well calibrated quantiles out of the box. More compute at prediction time (a GPU is recommended in production). Results on public datasets may be optimistic.
    Statistical (AutoARIMA, AutoETS) Simple, interpretable and with parametric intervals. Behind machine learning and foundation models in the three datasets: ETS cannot use exogenous variables, and a model per series cannot learn the patterns shared by many series. Fitting one model per series is also slow.
    Deep learning (LSTM) Competitive when it learns from many series at once, although its accuracy varies with the random seed. Needs plenty of data and tuning: with a single series it is at the level of the baseline or below.
    Baseline (seasonal naive) The reference: a model that does not beat it is not adding value.

    In short: start with two candidates, a machine learning model with good features and a foundation model, which forecasts without training, and always compare them with a baseline on your own data.

    How the models are compared¶

    • Same evaluation: in each dataset, all the models are evaluated on the same test period with the same TimeSeriesFold. Each family has its own backtesting function, but the partitions are identical. The models are trained once on the training set, without refitting between folds; Chronos-2, which is not trained, receives as context all the observations before each fold. It is used in its small version (autogluon/chronos-2-small, the default in skforecast), which runs fast on CPU; the base version (autogluon/chronos-2) is larger.

    • No tuning on the test set: each model uses a reasonable configuration (lags, features, hyperparameters, network size), fixed in advance and not searched on the test period. It is not the best possible configuration for each dataset: tuning it on a validation period, as shown in hyperparameter tuning, can improve any of the models.

    • Prediction intervals of 80%: each family uses its natural method. Conformal prediction with the out-of-sample residuals of a backtest before the test period for Ridge and LightGBM in the first two datasets, conformal prediction with in-sample residuals for the global models of the store sales dataset, the seasonal naive and the LSTM, the parametric intervals of ARIMA and ETS and the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles of Chronos-2. See probabilistic forecasting.

    • Metrics: MAE, MASE (the MAE divided by the MAE of the one-step naive forecast in the training set: lower is better and, being scale free, it can be compared across datasets and series), coverage of the interval (the closer to 80%, the better calibrated) and the time of the whole backtesting, on CPU. The first time ARIMA and ETS run in a new environment, numba compiles them once (a few seconds); the times shown were measured after that compilation.

    The backtesting predictions of every model are stored in a dictionary, with the same column names (pred, lower_bound, upper_bound and, for several series, level). Two small functions compute the metrics and plot the predictions from that dictionary.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    # Functions to summarize and plot the backtesting predictions
# ==============================================================================

# Order of the models in tables and figures
models = ["Seasonal naive", "Ridge", "LightGBM", "Chronos-2", "ARIMA", "ETS", "LSTM"]


def summarize(predictions, elapsed, series, n_train):
    """
    MAE, MASE, interval coverage and time of each model. MAE and coverage are
    computed over all the predicted values, MASE is the average of the series.
    """
    results = {}
    for model, pred in predictions.items():

        if "level" not in pred.columns:
            pred = pred.assign(level=series.columns[0])
        y_true = pd.concat(
            [series.loc[p.index, level] for level, p in pred.groupby("level")]
        )
        pred = pd.concat([p for _, p in pred.groupby("level")])

        mase = [
            mean_absolute_scaled_error(
                y_true  = series.loc[p.index, level],
                y_pred  = p["pred"],
                y_train = series[level].iloc[:n_train]
            )
            for level, p in pred.groupby("level")
        ]
        coverage = calculate_coverage(
                       y_true.to_numpy(),
                       pred["lower_bound"].to_numpy(),
                       pred["upper_bound"].to_numpy()
                   )

        results[model] = {
            "MAE": np.mean(np.abs(y_true.to_numpy() - pred["pred"].to_numpy())),
            "MASE": np.mean(mase),
            "Coverage (80%)": coverage,
            "Time (s)": elapsed[model],
        }

    return pd.DataFrame(results).T.sort_values("MASE")


def plot_predictions(predictions, series, level, title):
    """
    One panel per model with its backtesting predictions and interval.
    """
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(11, 4.5), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    for ax, model in zip(axes.flat, models):

        pred = predictions[model]
        if "level" in pred.columns:
            pred = pred.loc[pred["level"] == level]
        
        plot_prediction_intervals(
            predictions         = pred,
            y_true              = series,
            target_variable     = level,
            title               = model,
            kwargs_fill_between = {"color": "white", "alpha": 0.25, "zorder": 1},
            ax                  = ax
        )
        ax.get_legend().remove()
    
    handles, labels = axes.flat[0].get_legend_handles_labels()
    axes.flat[-1].axis("off")
    axes.flat[-1].legend(handles, labels, loc="center", frameon=False)
    fig.suptitle(title)
    fig.tight_layout()
    # Functions to summarize and plot the backtesting predictions # ============================================================================== # Order of the models in tables and figures models = ["Seasonal naive", "Ridge", "LightGBM", "Chronos-2", "ARIMA", "ETS", "LSTM"] def summarize(predictions, elapsed, series, n_train): """ MAE, MASE, interval coverage and time of each model. MAE and coverage are computed over all the predicted values, MASE is the average of the series. """ results = {} for model, pred in predictions.items(): if "level" not in pred.columns: pred = pred.assign(level=series.columns[0]) y_true = pd.concat( [series.loc[p.index, level] for level, p in pred.groupby("level")] ) pred = pd.concat([p for _, p in pred.groupby("level")]) mase = [ mean_absolute_scaled_error( y_true = series.loc[p.index, level], y_pred = p["pred"], y_train = series[level].iloc[:n_train] ) for level, p in pred.groupby("level") ] coverage = calculate_coverage( y_true.to_numpy(), pred["lower_bound"].to_numpy(), pred["upper_bound"].to_numpy() ) results[model] = { "MAE": np.mean(np.abs(y_true.to_numpy() - pred["pred"].to_numpy())), "MASE": np.mean(mase), "Coverage (80%)": coverage, "Time (s)": elapsed[model], } return pd.DataFrame(results).T.sort_values("MASE") def plot_predictions(predictions, series, level, title): """ One panel per model with its backtesting predictions and interval. """ fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(11, 4.5), sharex=True, sharey=True) for ax, model in zip(axes.flat, models): pred = predictions[model] if "level" in pred.columns: pred = pred.loc[pred["level"] == level] plot_prediction_intervals( predictions = pred, y_true = series, target_variable = level, title = model, kwargs_fill_between = {"color": "white", "alpha": 0.25, "zorder": 1}, ax = ax ) ax.get_legend().remove() handles, labels = axes.flat[0].get_legend_handles_labels() axes.flat[-1].axis("off") axes.flat[-1].legend(handles, labels, loc="center", frameon=False) fig.suptitle(title) fig.tight_layout()

    Which model wins with exogenous variables?¶

    Daily electricity demand in Victoria (Australia) from 2012 to 2014, with the maximum and mean temperature and the holidays as exogenous variables. The demand has a weekly and a yearly seasonality and depends strongly on the temperature. The last 56 days are predicted in 2 folds of 28 days.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    # Download data and aggregate it to daily values
# ==============================================================================
data = fetch_dataset(name="vic_electricity")
data["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(data["Date"])
data = data.groupby("Date").agg(
           demand    = ("Demand", "sum"),
           temp_max  = ("Temperature", "max"),
           temp_mean = ("Temperature", "mean"),
           holiday   = ("Holiday", "max"),
       )
data = data.loc["2012-01-01":"2014-12-31"].asfreq("D")
data.index.name = None
data["demand"] = data["demand"] / 1000  # MWh to GWh
data["holiday"] = data["holiday"].astype(float)
data.head(3)

y = data["demand"]
exog = data[["temp_max", "temp_mean", "holiday"]]
n_train = len(data) - 56

print(f"Train dates : {data.index[0].date()} --- {data.index[n_train - 1].date()}  (n={n_train})")
print(f"Test dates  : {data.index[n_train].date()} --- {data.index[-1].date()}  (n={len(data) - n_train})")

cv = TimeSeriesFold(
         steps              = 28,
         initial_train_size = n_train,
         refit              = False,
         verbose            = False
     )

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.5))
ax.plot(y.iloc[:n_train], label="train")
ax.plot(y.iloc[n_train:], label="test")
ax.set_title("Daily electricity demand (GWh)")
ax.legend();

    # Seasonal naive: the value of the same day of the previous week
# ==============================================================================
predictions, elapsed = {}, {}

start = time.perf_counter()
forecaster = ForecasterEquivalentDate(offset=7)
_, predictions["Seasonal naive"] = backtesting_forecaster(
    forecaster           = forecaster,
    y                    = y,
    cv                   = cv,
    metric               = "mean_absolute_error",
    interval             = [0.1, 0.9],
    interval_method      = "conformal",
    use_binned_residuals = False,
    show_progress        = False
)
elapsed["Seasonal naive"] = time.perf_counter() - start
    # Seasonal naive: the value of the same day of the previous week # ============================================================================== predictions, elapsed = {}, {} start = time.perf_counter() forecaster = ForecasterEquivalentDate(offset=7) _, predictions["Seasonal naive"] = backtesting_forecaster( forecaster = forecaster, y = y, cv = cv, metric = "mean_absolute_error", interval = [0.1, 0.9], interval_method = "conformal", use_binned_residuals = False, show_progress = False ) elapsed["Seasonal naive"] = time.perf_counter() - start
    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    # Machine learning: Ridge and LightGBM with lags, rolling mean, calendar features
# and exogenous variables. Intervals use the out-of-sample residuals of a backtest
# over the year before the test period.
# ==============================================================================
cv_calibration = TimeSeriesFold(
                     steps              = 28,
                     initial_train_size = n_train - 365,
                     refit              = False,
                     verbose            = False
                 )
estimators = {
    "Ridge": Ridge(),
    "LightGBM": LGBMRegressor(
                    n_estimators  = 400,
                    learning_rate = 0.03,
                    num_leaves    = 15,
                    random_state  = 123,
                    verbose       = -1
                ),
}
for model, estimator in estimators.items():

    start = time.perf_counter()

    forecaster = ForecasterRecursive(
                     estimator         = estimator,
                     lags              = 7,
                     window_features   = RollingFeatures(stats="mean", window_sizes=7),
                     calendar_features = CalendarFeatures(features=["day_of_week", "day_of_year"]),
                     transformer_y     = StandardScaler(),
                     transformer_exog  = StandardScaler()
                 )
    
    _, pred_calibration = backtesting_forecaster(
        forecaster    = forecaster,
        y             = y.iloc[:n_train],
        exog          = exog.iloc[:n_train],
        cv            = cv_calibration,
        metric        = "mean_absolute_error",
        show_progress = False
    )
    
    forecaster.fit(y=y.iloc[:n_train], exog=exog.iloc[:n_train])
    forecaster.set_out_sample_residuals(
        y_true = y.loc[pred_calibration.index],
        y_pred = pred_calibration["pred"]
    )
    _, predictions[model] = backtesting_forecaster(
        forecaster              = forecaster,
        y                       = y,
        exog                    = exog,
        cv                      = cv,
        metric                  = "mean_absolute_error",
        interval                = [0.1, 0.9],
        interval_method         = "conformal",
        use_in_sample_residuals = False,
        use_binned_residuals    = False,
        show_progress           = False
    )
    
    elapsed[model] = time.perf_counter() - start
    # Machine learning: Ridge and LightGBM with lags, rolling mean, calendar features # and exogenous variables. Intervals use the out-of-sample residuals of a backtest # over the year before the test period. # ============================================================================== cv_calibration = TimeSeriesFold( steps = 28, initial_train_size = n_train - 365, refit = False, verbose = False ) estimators = { "Ridge": Ridge(), "LightGBM": LGBMRegressor( n_estimators = 400, learning_rate = 0.03, num_leaves = 15, random_state = 123, verbose = -1 ), } for model, estimator in estimators.items(): start = time.perf_counter() forecaster = ForecasterRecursive( estimator = estimator, lags = 7, window_features = RollingFeatures(stats="mean", window_sizes=7), calendar_features = CalendarFeatures(features=["day_of_week", "day_of_year"]), transformer_y = StandardScaler(), transformer_exog = StandardScaler() ) _, pred_calibration = backtesting_forecaster( forecaster = forecaster, y = y.iloc[:n_train], exog = exog.iloc[:n_train], cv = cv_calibration, metric = "mean_absolute_error", show_progress = False ) forecaster.fit(y=y.iloc[:n_train], exog=exog.iloc[:n_train]) forecaster.set_out_sample_residuals( y_true = y.loc[pred_calibration.index], y_pred = pred_calibration["pred"] ) _, predictions[model] = backtesting_forecaster( forecaster = forecaster, y = y, exog = exog, cv = cv, metric = "mean_absolute_error", interval = [0.1, 0.9], interval_method = "conformal", use_in_sample_residuals = False, use_binned_residuals = False, show_progress = False ) elapsed[model] = time.perf_counter() - start

    # Statistical: AutoARIMA with weekly seasonality and exogenous variables, and
# AutoETS with weekly seasonality (ETS does not use exogenous variables)
# ==============================================================================
start = time.perf_counter()
forecaster = ForecasterStats(
                 estimator = Arima(order=None, seasonal_order=None, m=7)
             )
_, predictions["ARIMA"] = backtesting_stats(
    forecaster        = forecaster,
    y                 = y,
    exog              = exog,
    cv                = cv,
    metric            = "mean_absolute_error",
    interval          = [0.1, 0.9],
    show_progress     = False,
    suppress_warnings = True
)
elapsed["ARIMA"] = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
forecaster = ForecasterStats(estimator=Ets(m=7))
_, predictions["ETS"] = backtesting_stats(
    forecaster        = forecaster,
    y                 = y,
    cv                = cv,
    metric            = "mean_absolute_error",
    interval          = [0.1, 0.9],
    show_progress     = False,
    suppress_warnings = True
)
elapsed["ETS"] = time.perf_counter() - start
    # Statistical: AutoARIMA with weekly seasonality and exogenous variables, and # AutoETS with weekly seasonality (ETS does not use exogenous variables) # ============================================================================== start = time.perf_counter() forecaster = ForecasterStats( estimator = Arima(order=None, seasonal_order=None, m=7) ) _, predictions["ARIMA"] = backtesting_stats( forecaster = forecaster, y = y, exog = exog, cv = cv, metric = "mean_absolute_error", interval = [0.1, 0.9], show_progress = False, suppress_warnings = True ) elapsed["ARIMA"] = time.perf_counter() - start start = time.perf_counter() forecaster = ForecasterStats(estimator=Ets(m=7)) _, predictions["ETS"] = backtesting_stats( forecaster = forecaster, y = y, cv = cv, metric = "mean_absolute_error", interval = [0.1, 0.9], show_progress = False, suppress_warnings = True ) elapsed["ETS"] = time.perf_counter() - start

    # Foundation: Chronos-2 zero-shot, with the exogenous variables as covariates
# ==============================================================================
start = time.perf_counter()
forecaster = ForecasterFoundation(
                 estimator = FoundationModel("autogluon/chronos-2-small", device_map="cpu")
             )

_, pred = backtesting_foundation(
    forecaster    = forecaster,
    series        = y,
    exog          = exog,
    cv            = cv,
    metric        = "mean_absolute_error",
    quantiles     = [0.1, 0.5, 0.9],
    show_progress = False
)
predictions["Chronos-2"] = pred.rename(
    columns={"q_0.1": "lower_bound", "q_0.5": "pred", "q_0.9": "upper_bound"}
)
elapsed["Chronos-2"] = time.perf_counter() - start

    • LightGBM, with lags, calendar features and the temperature, is the most accurate model. Chronos-2 comes close without any training, using the temperature and the holidays as covariates.

    • The features carry most of the information: the models that cannot use the temperature (ETS) or that learn from a single series with little data (LSTM) are at the level of the baseline.

    • With out-of-sample residuals, the intervals of the machine learning models reach the nominal coverage or exceed it. The interval of ETS, which does not use the temperature, is very wide.

    What if the series is short?¶

    Monthly expenditure on corticosteroid drugs in Australia (h2o dataset): only 204 observations, with trend and yearly seasonality and no exogenous variables. The last 36 months are predicted in 3 folds of 12 months.

    # Machine learning: Ridge and LightGBM with 24 lags and the month. Intervals use
# the out-of-sample residuals of a backtest over the 3 years before the test period.
# ==============================================================================
cv_calibration = TimeSeriesFold(
                     steps              = 12,
                     initial_train_size = n_train - 36,
                     refit              = False,
                     verbose            = False
                 )
estimators = {
    "Ridge": Ridge(),
    "LightGBM": LGBMRegressor(
                    n_estimators  = 200,
                    learning_rate = 0.05,
                    max_depth     = 4,
                    random_state  = 123,
                    verbose       = -1
                ),
}
for model, estimator in estimators.items():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    forecaster = ForecasterRecursive(
                     estimator         = estimator,
                     lags              = 24,
                     calendar_features = CalendarFeatures(features=["month"]),
                     transformer_y     = StandardScaler(),
                     binner_kwargs     = {"n_bins": 3}  # Few calibration residuals to store by bin
                 )
    
    _, pred_calibration = backtesting_forecaster(
        forecaster    = forecaster,
        y             = y.iloc[:n_train],
        cv            = cv_calibration,
        metric        = "mean_absolute_error",
        show_progress = False
    )

    forecaster.fit(y=y.iloc[:n_train])
    forecaster.set_out_sample_residuals(
        y_true = y.loc[pred_calibration.index],
        y_pred = pred_calibration["pred"]
    )
    _, predictions[model] = backtesting_forecaster(
        forecaster              = forecaster,
        y                       = y,
        cv                      = cv,
        metric                  = "mean_absolute_error",
        interval                = [0.1, 0.9],
        interval_method         = "conformal",
        use_in_sample_residuals = False,
        use_binned_residuals    = False,
        show_progress           = False
    )
    elapsed[model] = time.perf_counter() - start

    • With little history, the pre-trained knowledge of Chronos-2 makes the difference: it is the most accurate model without any training.

    • The machine learning models, with lags and the month as features, come next. The statistical models are at the level of the seasonal naive.

    • The LSTM is the least accurate model: a neural network needs more data than a single short series provides.

    Many series: one global model or one model per series?¶

    Daily sales of 50 products in one store from 2013 to 2017 (store_sales dataset): 50 series of 1826 observations with weekly and yearly seasonality. The series are very regular and share the same patterns. Ridge, LightGBM, Chronos-2 and the LSTM are global models: a single model forecasts all the series. The seasonal naive, ARIMA and ETS are local models: one model is fitted for each series. The last 112 days are predicted in 4 folds of 28 days.

    In [20]:
    Copied!

series.columns = [f"item_{item}" for item in series.columns]
series = series.astype(float)
series.index.name = None
series.columns.name = None
n_train = len(series) - 112

print(f"Number of series: {series.shape[1]}")

cv = TimeSeriesFold(
         steps              = 28,
         initial_train_size = n_train,

    • When the series share the same patterns, the global models learn them from all the series at once: Chronos-2, LightGBM, the LSTM and Ridge are clearly more accurate than one AutoARIMA or one AutoETS per series.

    • Chronos-2 is the most accurate model without any training. The accuracy of the LSTM varies with the random seed: with other seeds, it is at the level of Ridge.

    • The global models are also much cheaper: they forecast all the series in seconds, while fitting one statistical model per series takes minutes. The coverage of all the intervals is close to the nominal level.

    Summary: accuracy and computation time¶

    The bars show the MASE of each model in the three datasets (lower is better), colored by family. The dashed line marks the seasonal naive: a model to its left adds value over the baseline. The time of the whole backtesting, on CPU, is shown in brackets.

for ax, (name, results) in zip(axes, datasets.items()):

    ax.barh(
        models, results["MASE"], height=0.65,
        color=[colors[families[model]] for model in models]
    )
    ax.axvline(
        results.loc["Seasonal naive", "MASE"], color="white", linestyle="--",

        time_label = f"{seconds:.2g} s" if seconds < 10 else f"{seconds:.0f} s"
        ax.text(
            value + 0.03, model, f"{value:.2f}  ({time_label})", va="center", fontsize=8,
            bbox={"facecolor": ax.get_facecolor(), "edgecolor": "none", "pad": 1}
        )
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1.7)
    ax.set_xticks([0, 0.5, 1, 1.5])
    ax.set_xlabel("MASE (lower is better)")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
axes[0].invert_yaxis()
handles = [plt.Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, color=color) for color in colors.values()]
fig.legend(

)

    ⚠ Warning

    These results come from three datasets and one configuration per model; they show trends, not a universal ranking. Keep in mind that:

    • The datasets are public, so they may be part of the data used to pre-train the foundation models, which would make their results optimistic.
    • A machine learning model with good domain features and careful tuning can beat any of these results on a given dataset.
    • The test periods are short and each model is run once (with a single seed for the LSTM), so small differences in accuracy or coverage between models are not meaningful.
    • Foundation models are slower at prediction time and usually need a GPU in production. The times above were measured on CPU.

    Before choosing a model for your data, compare the candidates with backtesting on your own series, as done here.
